result:
`final.py` scores **76.1** on the search split (valid, about 18 ms against the reference's 1.34 s), using **8 of 24** scorer calls.

| | search score | my held-out seeds (local) |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 | 1.0 |
| first champion (c1) | 67.7 | — |
| final (`final.py`) | 76.1 (earlier runs of the same algorithm: 74.3–86.5) | 67.8, all pairs exact |

The scores are noisy because the laptop is shared. The reference's own time moved between 1.34 and 1.63 s across calls, so differences under about 10% don't mean much. The held-out column comes from local generator seeds I never tuned on. The real held-out instances can only be scored by you.

**Why it's faster.** The baseline compares every pair of records. The final version only compares records that could possibly reach 80%:
- **Identical word sets are grouped first.** All pairs within a group are reported directly, and each distinct set is compared only once.
- **Rarest words first.** Each record's words are sorted from rarest to most common across the catalogue. Two records can only reach 80% if they share one of their first few rarest words, so only records sharing one of those are compared.
- **Fewer words go into the lookup index.** Records are handled smallest first, so each one only needs to add its first ⌈|B|/9⌉-ish rarest words to the index.
- **Size cut-off.** Records less than 0.8 times the current size are deleted from the front of each index list once and never looked at again.
- **Words that appear in only one record are never indexed.**
- **Exact check.** Every candidate pair still goes through the same integer test as the specification (`9·|A∩B| ≥ 4·(|A|+|B|)`, the same as `5·|A∩B| ≥ 4·|A∪B|`).

Correctness was checked against the reference on 300+ small edge-case inputs, 400 more random inputs, and 9 inputs of 3,000 records.

**Approaches tried** (my harness: generator plus the reference as oracle; it ranked c1 below c3 below c5 the same way the scorer did):

| candidate | change | harness | scorer | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | rarest-word index, set of candidates | 53× | 67.7 | becomes the base |
| c2 | C-level counting, skip one-off words | 54× | — | small gain |
| c3 | index fewer words per record | 59× | 75.1 | kept |
| c4 | index split by (word, size) | 58× | — | dropped: worse on long records |
| c5 | bisect-based size cut-off | 64× | 76.5 | kept |
| c6/c7 | private `_collections`/`_bisect` modules, front deletion | 65× | **invalid** | dropped: the static check bans private modules |
| c8 | c5 with front deletion instead of bisect | 67× | 79.6 | kept |
| c9 | verify candidates in a list comprehension | same | — | dropped: noise |
| c10/c11 | precomputed prefixes, faster rank build | same | 86.5 (noisy) | c11 is the final pick |
| c12 | candidate pairs from word buckets | 37× | — | dropped: too many pairs |
| c13 | skip the set when only one list is hit | same | — | dropped |

I also changed `final.py` to use `.get` instead of `__getitem__`. The scorer accepted the dunder, but the task says dunder attributes are rejected, so a stricter final check could have failed it.

**Budget:** I used the skill's default of about 15 minutes and 24 calls. I stopped after about 9 minutes and 8 calls, which is earlier than the skill asks. From c8 on, timings of c5, c8, c10 and c11 were within 1.5% of each other. What remains is mostly splitting the records into word sets (about 7 ms), which is unavoidable.

Candidate files c1–c13, `harness.py` and `prof.py` are in the folder, and `calls.log` lists every scorer call.
